statement: Policy Plus is a Windows desktop editor for Group Policy administrative-template settings. It loads policy definition files into a searchable tree and reads or writes values in the live registry, user profiles or policy files. Administrators and power users use it, including on Windows Home, which lacks the built-in editor.

The program has no users or roles of its own; Windows decides access. It requests the highest rights the signed-in user has, so changing machine policy needs an administrator. It tests writability and marks sources unmodifiable, and takes folder ownership only when an administrator downloads definitions.

It runs on the user's own Windows machine as a single desktop program on .NET Framework 4.x, editing that machine's registry and policy files. It hosts no service; its only outside call is the optional definitions download from Microsoft. That it is limited to administrator desktops is our assumption.

statement: As administrator, the program can load another user's registry file into the machine registry, from a profile folder list or a path the user chooses. It is administrator-only and rests on user-chosen paths, with no further check.

subject: system
statement: A typed user identifier for a policy source is joined into a file path under the system folder and written to, without checking its form. A crafted value could point the write elsewhere.

subject: system
statement: Every web request, including the installer download, permits the deprecated TLS 1.0 and 1.1 beside 1.2, to keep Windows Vista working. A weaker protocol could be negotiated; the code does not show an older version actually being used.

subject: system
statement: The program is built for .NET Framework 4.5.2, whose Microsoft support has ended. Findings differ on weight: newer Windows runs it on a still-supported 4.x runtime, so the exposure is the old build target, not the runtime in use.

subject: system
statement: The policy-version file is rewritten in place after being read. A failure midway leaves it truncated, so Windows may not notice a policy change.

subject: system
statement: Results of enabling privileges and loading a registry file are ignored. If either fails the program carries on without saying why, and a later save can fail or be silently skipped.

subject: system
statement: The ADMX download and unpack have no timeout or cancel, and the dialog refuses to close while they run. A stalled connection or hung installer leaves the dialog and its owner window unusable until the process is killed.

subject: system
statement: The download address and the folder inside the package are pinned to one release, Windows 11 26H2, on Microsoft's download site. If Microsoft moves the file or renames the folder, the download fails until the code is edited; later releases are not picked up.

subject: system
statement: The ADMX download trusts a Microsoft installer package on HTTPS alone: this code checks no hash or signature. A substituted package, or a compromised trust store or proxy, would put attacker-chosen definitions into the destination. Reach is this download only.

subject: system
statement: What an altered package could overwrite: the top-level definition files and the current-language and English folders replace same-named files in the chosen destination, by default the Windows policy folder, so every policy editor reading it would see the altered definitions.

subject: system
statement: The installer program is launched by bare name, so the system search order, not the code, decides which executable runs. A planted program earlier in that order would run instead.

subject: system
statement: When the ADMX download fails, the person sees only a generic message naming the phase; the cause is discarded. The scratch folder, under a fixed name, is left behind, so leftovers can sit in the next run's unpack target.

subject: system
statement: Saving can end with a Success message although sources were skipped as not writable. The box names each one as not writable, but the headline still says success, so a person may believe an edit to such a source was kept.

subject: system
statement: If the settings storage cannot be created or written, saved choices silently do not persist and the person is not told. Only a preference is lost, not policy edits.

subject: system
statement: The ADMX download deletes each same-named file before moving its replacement, and the sequence is not atomic. A failure part-way can leave the destination, by default the system policy folder, with a mix of old and new files and ownership already changed, with nothing rolled back.

subject: system
statement: A failed save of a comment is ignored without telling the person, so a note they typed can be lost while they believe it was kept.

subject: system
statement: Policy Plus is a Windows desktop editor for Group Policy administrative-template settings. It loads policy definition files into a searchable tree and reads or writes values in the live registry, user profiles or policy files. Administrators and power users use it, including on Windows Home, which lacks the built-in editor.

subject: system
statement: It runs on the user's own Windows machine as a single desktop program on .NET Framework 4.x, editing that machine's registry and policy files. It hosts no service; its only outside call is the optional definitions download from Microsoft. Limiting it to administrator desktops is our assumption.

subject: system
statement: A person launches the program, which opens the main window; closing that window ends it. On start it loads the saved definitions folder and policy sources from the user's registry; on close it releases any mounted registry hives.

subject: system
statement: Work begins only when a person uses the window: menu choices, double-clicking a policy and dialog buttons. There are no command-line arguments, network listeners or other programs calling in. A first-run prompt may also start the ADMX definitions download.

subject: system
statement: No scheduled or batch work exists. Everything runs when a person acts; the only background threads are the ADMX download and the policy search, each started by a button.

subject: system
statement: The program has no users or roles of its own; Windows decides access. It requests the highest rights the signed-in user has, so changing machine policy needs an administrator. It marks unwritable sources unmodifiable, and takes folder ownership only when an administrator downloads definitions.

subject: system
statement: Not applicable: it is a single-user desktop tool with no customers or organisations. It can edit another Windows user's policies only by loading that person's registry file or per-user policy folder by hand.

subject: system
statement: The program keeps its few preferences (last definitions folder, last policy sources, first-run flag) in the current user's registry under a Policy Plus key. It holds no secrets and no configuration file beyond the runtime version pin.

subject: system
statement: Failures are shown in message boxes; nothing is logged to a file or service and nothing is retried. Some errors are deliberately swallowed: unreadable saved sources fall back to local defaults, a failed settings key means preferences are not kept, and a comment-file error is ignored.

subject: system
statement: A developer builds in Visual Studio, with a batch script stamping the Git version first. A GitHub workflow runs on every push to master or on demand, builds the Release executable and uploads it, unsigned, to an Amazon S3 bucket as the latest build. One fact calls the workflow's release target unreadable; the other reads it, so that is stale. No test step exists.

subject: system
statement: One edit: the person opens a policy, the dialog changes an in-memory copy, then File | Save writes it, plus the comments file, and remembers the chosen sources in the settings key. Only writable sources are saved. Local policy is written to file, then Windows policy is refreshed where Group Policy exists; on Windows Home the difference is copied into the registry and a setting-change message broadcast. Another user's policy folder is written and refreshed. A policy file is only written; the live registry is already applied; an offline user hive applies on close.

subject: system
statement: Nothing runs around every action: no sign-in, request pipeline or interceptor. The program is attached to an application manifest that Windows reads at launch; the facts beneath leave its content unstated. When policy sources open and when saving, the program checks and reports whether each source is writable.
